Date: Mon, 24 Aug 2026 13:12:00 -0400
Subject: Post-call recap: Perf SLOs + Autoscaling needs

Thanks again for the demo earlier — appreciate you and the team walking us through Redwood's runtime. Quick recap from our side and a few open items so we can qualify next steps: 

- SLO targets: 95th percentile latency for text-gen should be <= 200ms for typical 256-token prompts; 99th percentile ideally < 500ms.
- Throughput: baseline 500 req/s, with burst capacity up to 1,500 req/s during peak payroll windows (30–45 min spikes).
- Concurrency: we expect sustained concurrency of ~600 concurrent active sessions, some of which use streaming partial responses (server-side streaming).
- Streaming: client expects chunked/streamed tokens for UX; need to confirm any impact on autoscale behavior.
- Warm pools & scale-up: we need clarity on how long spin-up takes and whether warm pools can be held for scheduled bursts.
- Queueing behavior: we cannot tolerate request queueing that pushes p95 beyond 200ms — acceptable only if we have backpressure and fallbacks (lower-capacity model variant).

Next steps we'd like from Redwood: a short note outlining how your autoscaling/burst model handles warm pools, expected cold start times, recommended warm pool sizing for our workload, and any constraints around streaming/long-poll connections. Also attach any perf measurements for similar customers if available.

Thanks,
Sarah
Sr. Engineering Manager, FastPay

Thanks for the clear recap, Sarah — this is very helpful. Looping in Dev (solutions engineer) and Rachel (AE) so we can capture technical details and propose a follow-up scope. High-level responses below; Dev will add specifics and numbers.

High-level answers / proposed next steps:
- Autoscale model: Redwood supports a mix of warm pools + reactive scale-up. For identified peak windows we recommend a small reserved warm pool and reactive burst capacity to handle unexpected spikes.
- Cold-starts & scale-up: cold model instance startup varies by model size and infra; typical scale-up latency to a ready warm instance is ~20–45s on dedicated pools, and 60–120s if launching new instances in hosted multi-tenant pools. We'll provide measured numbers for the model families you plan to use.
- Warm pool sizing: initial suggestion: warm pool to cover ~30–40% of expected burst (so for 1,500 req/s burst, warm pool suffices for ~450–600 rps). Dev, please confirm memory/slot sizing assumptions for FastPay's concurrency mix.
- Streaming: streaming connections keep KV cache warm per session; long-lived streams consume slots and should be accounted for in concurrency planning. We can route streaming requests to a streaming-optimized pool to reduce per-session footprint.
- Queueing & fallbacks: Redwood supports per-route queueing with deadlines and automatic fallback to smaller (lower-cost) model variants when queues exceed thresholds — we can enforce SLO guardrails rather than accumulating latency.

Attachments: I'll attach a short tech notes doc from Dev with more details. Proposed next steps: Dev and I will send a short sizing proposal and a 30-min follow-up to validate numbers and run a quick RPS test. Are you available Thurs 08/27 or Fri 08/28?

Best,

Thanks, Sarah — adding the technical details you asked for and a couple of clarifying questions. Attaching a short tech note (redwood-autoscale-tech-notes.pdf) that includes numbers and assumptions.

Key assumptions I used for the initial sizing:
- Target model family: small-to-medium LLMs (7B-13B) with typical per-request compute of ~80ms-120ms on a warmed GPU slot.
- Slot capacity: one warm slot can sustain ~20–30 concurrent streaming sessions or ~80–120 short non-streaming requests/sec depending on prompt length.
- Warm pool behavior: warm slots maintain model weights and KV cache; reusing warm slots keeps p95 stable. Warm slots are billed while reserved.
- Reactive scale-up: when traffic exceeds warm pool, we spin up additional instances; spin-up time to register a new slot in the pool is ~25–90s depending on infrared (shorter on Dedicated).
- Queueing & deadlines: we recommend short queue windows (100–250ms) with early fallback to a smaller model or cached responses for critical paths.

Clarifying questions:
1) Which exact model family(s) do you plan to use in production? (helps refine per-slot RPS)
2) For streaming sessions, what's the average session duration and average tokens per session?
3) For scheduled burst windows (payroll), do you want guaranteed reserved capacity (we can size a reserved pool) or prefer cost-efficient on-demand with warm pool + proactive warm-up?

Proposed tests:
- A 15-min RPS ramp test that simulates baseline -> peak -> sustained burst, while we monitor p95/p99 and queueing behavior. We can run this against a dedicated short-lived pool to get deterministic numbers.

I'll attach the tech note and a sample sizing sheet (FastPay-autoscale-SLA-request.xlsx) with editable assumptions.

Best,
Dev Patel
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

2) Streaming sessions: average duration ~45s, average tokens per session ~150; peak sessions may go up to 3–4 mins with ~500 tokens.
3) Scheduled burst approach: we'd like a hybrid — reserved warm pool for the payroll windows (predictable), plus reactive capacity for unexpected bursts. For payroll we can commit to reserved capacity for the 40–45 minute windows.

We can commit to a follow-up RPS validation test. Thurs 08/27 11:00am ET works for our team. Please send a calendar invite.
